PGE and Ãrsted successfully conclude monopile installation 23 Aug 2026 All monopiles have now been installed at the Baltica 2 offshore construction site – 107 for wind turbines and 4 for offshore substations. PGE and Ørsted completed this key stage on schedule. The efficient delivery of one of the most demanding offshore operations was the result of precise planning, effective coordination of the works and experience in delivering large-scale offshore projects. The Baltica 2 monopiles are up to 100 metres long, between 7.5 and 10.5 metres in diameter and weigh around 1,900 tonnes. The installation of each monopile was a complex logistical operation requiring precise coordination of the production and transport process, appropriate preparation of the installation site, the availability of specialist vessels, and suitable weather conditions. Planning that translated into pace Before the work began, the Baltica 2 project team conducted a detailed analysis of different delivery options and potential scenarios that could affect the installation process. The preparations drew on Ørsted’s experience in delivering offshore wind projects across multiple markets, as well as the expertise of Van Oord, which is responsible for carrying out this stage of the work. This enabled the Baltica 2 project team to develop solutions designed to minimise key risks related to factors including the installation sequence, the availability of components and installation vessels, logistics, and the coordination of offshore activities. Greater flexibility through two installation vessels An important element of the plan was the deployment of two Van Oord specialist installation vessels – Svanen and Aeolus. By combining the capabilities of both vessels with its offshore wind installation expertise, the project team was able to increase installation capacity, optimise the sequence of offshore works and provide greater flexibility throughout the campaign. The integrated approach helped the teams maintain momentum, respond effectively to changing offshore conditions and complete the monopile installation campaign on schedule. ' Completing the campaign on schedule shows how important thorough preparation and the management of dependencies between successive stages of work are in offshore construction. For Baltica 2, it was crucial to plan logistics, vessel operations and the installation sequence in a way that limited the risk of downtime while maintaining operational flexibility. This successful delivery was made possible by a strong team whose expertise, commitment and close collaboration kept the campaign on track. Experience gained by Ørsted through the delivery of more than 30 offshore wind projects across three continents helps us identify potential bottlenecks early and respond before they begin to affect the schedule of the entire project' said Ulrik Lange, Managing Director Baltica 2 at Ørsted . ' Baltica 2 is currently the largest investment project being delivered by the PGE Group and one of the most important energy transition projects in Poland. Each stage completed on schedule confirms how crucial the consistent and comprehensive preparation of this undertaking is. Alongside the offshore work, we are intensively developing the onshore infrastructure, including the facilities required to transmit power from the wind farm to the National Power System, as well as the operations and maintenance base. These are key elements of the overall project that will ensure the efficient and safe operation of the offshore wind farm for decades to come' said Patrycja Kunc - Rozbrój, Executive Vice President of the Management Board of PGE Baltica . ' Completing the monopile installation campaign for Baltica 2 safely and on schedule is an important milestone for the project and for Poland’s offshore wind ambitions. We are proud to have contributed our offshore wind expertise, specialist vessels and experienced project teams to this complex operation. The close collaboration with Ørsted was key to maintaining progress and delivering this phase successfully' said Maurits den Broeder, Managing Director Offshore Energy at Van Oord . Next stages of offshore construction The completion of monopile installation marks the end of one of the most important stages in the construction of the offshore part of Baltica 2. In parallel, secondary structures required for the future operation of the wind farm are being installed on the completed foundations. In total, more than 400 units will be installed on the foundations, including anode cages protecting the foundations against corrosion, boat landings for service vessels, and internal and external platforms. 75% of these units are manufactured at facilities in Poland. The installation of the secondary steel structures is expected to continue until the end of 2026. At the same time, preparations are under way for the installation of further wind farm components: offshore substations and export cables later this year, followed by inter-array cables and wind turbines in 2027. According to the project schedule, first power from Baltica 2 is expected in the first half of 2027, with full commercial operation planned by the end of 2027. About Baltica 2 Baltica 2 is a 1.5 GW offshore wind farm developed as a joint venture by PGE Polska Grupa Energetyczna and Ørsted. In terms of generation capacity, it is one of the largest energy investments currently being developed in Poland and one of the key offshore wind projects in the Baltic Sea. Once completed, Baltica 2 will be able to supply renewable energy to around 2.5 million households in Poland . The offshore wind farm under construction is also one of the key investments strengthening Poland’s energy security. Its delivery will increase the share of renewable energy in the national energy mix and reduce dependence on fossil fuels. At the same time, the project is driving the development of the Polish economy - from ports and infrastructure to the domestic supply chain and new jobs. It is an investment that is truly laying the foundations for Poland’s offshore sector for decades to come. Baltica 2 is being built approximately 40 km off the coast near Ustka and is scheduled to be commissioned in 2027. The project has all the required permits and a 25-year Contract for Difference (CfD) . Photograph: Annika Karlbom/Hallands Nyheter View image in fullscreen Mark Smith with his wife, Petra, was told he was an ‘alien’ without permission to stay. Photograph: Annika Karlbom/Hallands Nyheter UK news Briton threatened with deportation from Sweden over Brexit rules goes into hiding Mark Smith, who has severe health issues, says he was told three times he needed to do nothing in order to remain after Brexit Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error. Mark Smith, 60, who has had heart attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay. Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said. A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”. View image in fullscreen Mark Smith and his wife, Petra, have moved out of their apartment in Falkenberg to caravan park. Photograph: Annika Karlbom/Hallands Nyheter Smith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay after Brexit in 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules. He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain. Other countries, such as Spain, did not opt for that system and just required Britons to declare they were a resident. Smith said: “I asked the tax authorities three times on different occasions if I had to do anything because of Brexit and they said no, telling me I had to wait for five years to apply for permanent residency. “Because it was the tax authority, a government body, I took it for granted that what they told me was correct,” he added. David Milstead , a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights activist working through the Brits in Sweden group, said Smith’s case was typical of many Britons living in Sweden. View image in fullscreen Smith has been in Sweden since 2017. He worked, had private health insurance, and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority. Milstead said: “Mark’s experience is far from unusual. I have encountered many British citizens who actively sought information from the Swedish authorities about their residence rights after Brexit, only to receive vague, unhelpful answers, sometimes being told that they needed to do nothing.” They include the 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas , whose husband also inquired about Brexit residency and was told by the tax authorities there was nothing to do, and who is now fighting a removal order. Smith had a minor heart attack on Wednesday night but wanted his situation publicised because he said the British government needed to know what was happening to expats in Sweden, “not just to me but others”. His wife, Petra, said his health conditions had left him so vulnerable she was not sure “if he will last until Christmas”. She said: “He has been told he can’t drive, he can’t fly – what do they expect him to do? Get up and walk to England? Come on, Sweden, we need to step back from all of this and be better.” After 12 years together, she said deportation would be devastating for her and her 15-year-old son who has special needs, who Smith co-parents. “It is wrong what they are doing, I feel ashamed to be Swedish. What they are doing is racist to British people,” Petra said. View image in fullscreen Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he applied for sickness benefit and was told by officials he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. Milstead said Smith’s case was “depressingly familiar” and should warrant the urgent attention of the European Commission, which has previously said Sweden was not breaking any laws. “A gentleman with Mark’s serious health conditions should not be having to fight deportation. It is difficult to understand how the European Commission has concluded that Sweden’s treatment of late applications under the [Brexit] withdrawal agreement does not warrant a challenge,” he said. “Sweden stands out so starkly from other EU countries, and there are serious questions that remain unanswered, particularly about proportionality and the treatment of vulnerable people. These are precisely the kinds of cases where the protections of the withdrawal agreement ought to matter most.” The Scandinavian country has found itself under mounting pressure over its approach to the withdrawal agreements having deported 458 Britons , including one man who had been in the country since he was 10 years old, and a 65-year-old man married to a Swede with no family or property in the UK. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Sweden has also issued removal orders to a man with dementia who is in 24-hour care and who has been in the country for 25 years. Under the legally binding treaty, it was agreed governments would communicate the Brexit residency rules, consider late applications on reasonable grounds, and exercise “proportionate” decisions including in the case of vulnerable people. Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he started to get ill and applied for sickness benefit. He was told by officials that he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. The couple immediately did so; they recall making the application at the end of 2021, in time for Sweden’s 31 December 2021 deadline. They waited more than two years to hear back and when they did it was a rejection on the grounds that they were not married and therefore did not have a family connection to merit his residency in Sweden. Mark Smith and Petra on their wedding day in Sweden in 2023. Photograph: Supplied They were married in 2023 and had been living together since 2017. It is not clear if Smith applied for the specific Brexit residency or through the usual immigration route, an important difference and one that may not have been made clear to British protected by the withdrawal agreement. Family connections are not a criteria under free movement rights, which apply to any individual regardless of marital status, so campaigners believe they have a strong case. Smith said: “We were so much in love, we lived together, we did everything together, even now we hold hands walking down the streets. We wanted to get married, we wanted to do it the right way. I wanted to ask Petra’s father for permission and have him give her away, but two weeks after he gave me permission to marry his daughter, he passed. “So we were looking into marriage but things just kept happening. But we don’t understand why this matters.” They also said they had not been given the full court paperwork from the first case appealing against the migration agency’s decision, so they appealed to a higher courtwithout the full arguments against them. After speaking to a judge this week, Petra has had assurances that all the paperwork will be sent to them by post, but they feel angry that they were not apprised of the information that the migration agency was arguing before the courts. Sweden’s migration agency has said there is no evidence Sweden has taken an extreme approach to the withdrawal agreement. The UK Foreign Office has raised concerns about Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement with the European Commission on numerous occasions, but has been told Sweden is not breaching the agreement. A spokesperson said: “We are in touch with Mr Smith and are providing consular support. We know this is a distressing and challenging time for those concerned and we are urgently raising the situation with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission.” The Foreign Office welcomed a statement by Sweden’s former migration minister Johan Forssell in August that Sweden would examine “additional measures” that would address the issue of Brexit deportation, and a similar declaration by Magdalena Andersson, who is on track to form the new government.
